consensus_summary: The garden primarily symbolizes paradise (Eden) as the place of God’s presence, unbroken fellowship, divine provision, and eschatological restoration, framing the biblical storyline from creation to new creation; complementary alternatives include temple/sanctuary, bride/soul, fruitful spiritual life, and Gethsemane typology.
book_summary: A planted grouping of trees, specifically nations or peoples arranged together under a gardener’s rule.
consensus_core_identification: Paradise/Eden as the place of divine presence and fellowship with God (lost and restored).
book_core_identification: Planted grouping of trees standing for nations/peoples under a gardener’s rule.
boundary_disagreement: Consensus extensions cover Eden, Gethsemane, Song garden, watered garden, and garden-tomb as paradise/presence/fruitfulness motifs; the book’s national-political grouping under a ruler is outside those bounds entirely.
material_contradiction: None directly; the book’s identification is simply absent from the consensus primary meaning and listed alternatives rather than negating paradise language.
rationale: Minimum cores differ in referent: consensus centers on Edenic paradise/presence, while the book centers on a collective of trees-as-nations under rule. No consensus primary or alternative meaning matches or refines into the book’s national-arrangement reading, so the relation is novelty by absence. The book’s own common-view note explicitly flags the paradise reading as the familiar teaching it is setting aside.
strongest_objection: Ezekiel 31:9 places ‘trees of Eden’ inside ‘the garden of God,’ treating the garden as the containing locale rather than equating it with the planted grouping of nations itself; the verse therefore supplies at best remote background for a trees=nations motif, not direct warrant for redefining Garden.
